why: A stranger reads 'I worked it out' for 1,100 words before learning who 'I' is; the page's own first sentence of 'How far to trust this' is brought up as a signpost. 'Folded at the foot' is a private phrase and shares no word with the label the reader will actually see, so the label is quoted.

old: Cut the Earth in two through its centre, as you would halve an orange. Of all the ways to make the cut, which leaves the most land on one side? The answer usually quoted is the half centred near Nantes, in the west of France. I worked it out from open data and got a half centred in the sea off Catalonia instead. Then I found that the same answer had been in print since 2003.
new: Cut the Earth into two equal parts, as you would halve an orange. Of all the ways to make the cut, which leaves the most land on one side? A half is named by the point at the middle of its surface, its centre. The answer usually quoted is the half centred near Nantes, in the west of France. I worked it out from freely available data and got a half centred in the sea off Catalonia instead. Then I found that my answer had been in print since 2003. Further down, the same question is asked about people and about woodpeckers.
why: 'Centre' was used in two senses three sentences apart (the middle of the Earth, then a point on its surface) and the second was never explained; now the first is gone and the second is defined once. 'Open data' is a term of art. 'The same answer' could be read as the same as the usual one. The last sentence prepares the reader for the lower pair of globes in the first figure, which otherwise shows people before the text has mentioned them. The new sentence about the centre is a definition of the page's own word, not a finding; the second reader should still pass it.

old: A cross marks the centre of each half.
new: A cross marks the centre of each half. You can also turn the globe yourself.
why: The globe is the thing most likely to keep a stranger on the page, and it is first mentioned 1,000 words down. Same link as in 'Turn it yourself'; nothing new is claimed.

old: Nantes, or a small island off the coast nearby, from determinations made in 1945 and 1913.
new: Nantes, worked out in 1945, or Île Dumet, a small island off the coast nearby, worked out in 1913.
why: 'Determinations' is a surveyor's word, and the reader had to pair two places with two dates. The island is named here so that the label on the map means something when it comes. The pairing (Nantes 1945, Île Dumet 1913) and the island's name are taken from the story's own second caption.

old: From an open map of the world's coastlines

old: Loss of land, in percentage points of the world's land, when the centre is moved away from the best point. Nantes (Boggs, 1945) and Île Dumet (Berget, 1913), as Wikipedia gives them, are the two older determinations usually quoted; both lie beside the northern summit. Affholder's paper, described below, has a map of the same ridge (his figure 5).
new: The numbers on the lines say how much land is lost, as a percentage of the world's land, when the centre is moved there from the best point (marked "largest share"). Nantes (Boggs, 1945) and Île Dumet (Berget, 1913), as Wikipedia gives them, are the two older centres usually quoted; both lie beside the northern summit. The same ridge was already mapped in a paper of 2003, described below.
why: The old caption said 'loss' where the text said 'the darker, the more land', and never said that the numbers are the ones printed on the lines. 'Percentage points' is a statistician's phrase; a fall of so many points in the share is the same thing as that percentage of the world's land lost. The credit for the earlier map stays beside the figure but no longer uses a name the reader has not met. This drops '(his figure 5)' from the story: it is a checker's pointer, and the fold does not carry it yet (see needs-author.json). The names Boggs and Berget and 'as Wikipedia gives them' are kept because the fold does not carry them either.

old: The map shows what happened: the darker the blue, the more land a half centred there holds. Think of the share of land as a landscape, high wherever a centre does well. Between Catalonia and Brittany it forms a long ridge, nearly level and 800 km from end to end, with a summit at each end.
new: Between Catalonia and Brittany the landscape forms a long ridge, nearly level and 800 km from end to end, with a summit at each end: the two dark patches on the map.
why: The first two sentences have moved above the figure (summits-intro). 'What happened' pointed back across a heading and a figure to nothing in particular. The added words tell the reader where on the map to look; they describe the figure and claim nothing more.

old: What is left over favours Catalonia.
new: What is left over is that 46,000 km², and it favours Catalonia.
why: Ties the remainder to the one figure the reader has already been given for it. This is arithmetic, not a new claim: the difference between the two halves is what is gained less what is lost.

old: It mentions a study that found two such points, one in Brittany and one between the Balearic Islands and Catalonia. The study is by Jean-Georges Affholder of France's national mapping agency, and it was published in 2003. Working from his agency's own coastline, he found both summits, said that the Mediterranean one is the higher, and mapped the ridge between them. The two points he found first are within four kilometres of mine.
new: It mentions a study that found the same two summits, one in Brittany and one between the Balearic Islands and Catalonia. The study is by Jean-Georges Affholder of France's national mapping agency, and it was published in 2003. Working from his agency's own map of the coast, he said that the southern summit is the higher, and he mapped the ridge between the two. His two points, as he first worked them out, are within four kilometres of mine.
why: 'Two such points' had nothing for 'such' to point at. The finding of the two summits was told twice in three sentences; it is now told once ('the same two summits' stands for the old 'he found both summits'). 'The Mediterranean one' was a third name for what the page has called the southern summit. 'The two points he found first' can be read as 'he found them before I did'; the new wording keeps the limit on the claim (his first working, not his last) and makes it visible. See the report: this sentence quotes the closer of two distances.

old: A model wrote this page and no person has checked it. What stands in for a person is this. Before each run I wrote down what I expected and posted a fingerprint of the sheet where the two other instances on this machine could see it, so that I could not change my mind afterwards. Eleven of the seventeen things I expected held, and three of the six failures came from one assumption, that the centre was at Nantes. Fresh instances of the model, which had seen none of the work, then read the main programs, and another read the longer account below against Affholder's paper. new:
A model wrote this page and no person has checked it. What stands in for a person is this. Before each computation I wrote down what I expected and put a fingerprint of the sheet on record, so that I could not change my mind afterwards. Eleven of the seventeen things I expected proved right. Of the six that proved wrong, three came from one assumption, that the centre was at Nantes.

Fresh copies of the same model, which had seen none of the work, then read the main programs, and another compared the longer account at the foot of the page with Affholder's paper. They found mistakes, which have been corrected and are listed there.
why: This was the hardest paragraph on the page: 'run', 'instances', 'this machine' and 'fresh instances of the model' are private words, and it was 130 words without a break. Who could see the fingerprint is a checker's detail and is already under the fold; 'on record' says less, not more. 'Below' meant the fold here and 'later in the story' in the caption; it now says where. 'Compared with' is no stronger than 'read against'. Split in two at the natural joint.

old: Which summit is higher rests on a margin of four parts in ten thousand. It held on three coastlines and in Affholder's work, but every map of a coast is simplified, and a coast is not a fixed line. And the move of the people's centre from the Alps to Berlin is a statement about one dataset, which is itself a model of where people live.
new: Which summit is higher rests on that thin margin of 46,000 km². It held on three maps of the coast and in Affholder's work, but every map of a coast is simplified, and a coast is not a fixed line. And the move of the people's centre from the Alps to near Berlin is a statement about one set of population maps, which is itself an estimate of where people live.
why: The margin had three numbers on one page (46,000 km², 'about the area of Estonia', and 'four parts in ten thousand', the last without saying of what). It now has the one the reader has already met; 'thin' is the story's own word for it. 'To Berlin' was a little firmer than the story's 'a little west of Berlin' and 'near Berlin'. 'Model' was used in two senses in one section (the author, and the population maps); 'estimate' is offered as the plain word for the second, and the second reader should confirm it is no stronger.
